extracted.intended_audience: marketing researchers, content/viral_marketers, and social scientists studying online sharing
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and measure content characteristics that increase the probability that online articles (or marketing content) will be shared/'go viral', based on field analysis of New York Times articles and controlled lab experiments. Emphasizes the role of specific emotions, arousal, practical utility, and external prominence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arousal / activation
rubrics_metrics.description: Activation (arousal) drives social transmission: content that evokes high-arousal emotions is more likely to be shared, regardless of whether the emotion is positive or negative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the paper's primary mechanism: arousal mediates the effect of specific emotions on sharing (laboratory mediation tests and field results). High-arousal positive (e.g., awe, amusement) and negative (e.g., anger, anxiety) emotions boost sharing; low-arousal (deactivating) emotions like sadness reduce sharing. Empirical support comes from logistic regressions on NYT data and experiments (Studies 2–3).

rubrics_metrics.name: Valence (positivity vs negativity)
rubrics_metrics.description: More positive content is more viral: positive valence increases the likelihood content will be highly shared.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Valence matters but is not sufficient: the relationship between emotion and virality is more complex than valence alone because arousal moderates effects. The field analysis shows positive content is more likely to make the most-e-mailed list even after controlling for frequency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Awe (specific emotion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Awe (a positive, high-arousal emotion) increases the odds that an article will be highly shared.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Figure 2 reports that a one-standard-deviation increase in awe increases the odds of making the NYT most-e-mailed list by ~30%. Treated as an activating positive emotion consistent with the arousal mechanism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anger (specific emotion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Anger (a negative, high-arousal emotion) increases the odds that content will be shared.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Figure 2 reports a one-standard-deviation increase in anger increases odds by ~34%. Laboratory Study 2b (high- vs low-anger vignettes) showed higher reported sharing in high-anger conditions and found arousal mediates the effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anxiety (specific emotion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Anxiety (negative, activating) is positively associated with virality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Figure 2 reports a one-standard-deviation increase in anxiety increases odds by ~21%. Treated as an activating negative emotion in support of the arousal explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sadness (specific emotion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sadness (a deactivating/low-arousal emotion) decreases the likelihood content will be shared.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Figure 2 shows a one-standard-deviation increase in sadness reduces the odds of making the most-e-mailed list (around –16%). Laboratory Study 3 experimentally manipulated sadness and found reduced sharing; arousal mediated the negative effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amusement (specific emotion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Amusement (positive, high-arousal humor-like emotion) increases sharing likelihood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study 2a used high- vs low-amusement advertising vignettes (Jimmy Dean examples) and found higher reported sharing and higher arousal in the high-amusement condition; arousal mediated the effect on sharing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical value / usefulness
rubrics_metrics.description: Content with higher practical utility is more likely to be shared (increases virality).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Figure 2 indicates a one-standard-deviation increase in practical value is associated with roughly a 30% increase in odds of making the most-e-mailed list. Note: practical utility increases e-mail sharing but is marginally less likely to be blogged about (possible platform/format differences).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interest
rubrics_metrics.description: More interesting content is more viral.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Figure 2 reports interest increases the odds (about +25% per +1SD). 'Interesting' content likely aligns with motives to entertain or inform; measured in hand-coded article characteristics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surprise
rubrics_metrics.description: Surprising content increases the likelihood of being shared.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Figure 2 reports a one-standard-deviation increase in surprise increases odds by about 14%. Surprise is treated as a content characteristic that increases transmission, consistent with novelty/curiosity drivers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotionality (overall amount of emotion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pieces that evoke more emotion in general are more likely to be shared.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Figure 2 indicates emotionality is positively associated with virality (around +18% per +1SD). However, the type (activation vs deactivation) of emotion matters for direction of effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prominence / external visibility (time at top of home page)
rubrics_metrics.description: External drivers of attention—such as being featured prominently or spending more time as the lead story—substantially increase sharing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Figure 2 equates a one-standard-deviation increase in time at top of home page to about a 20% increase in odds of making the most-e-mailed list. The paper emphasizes that content characteristics are of similar importance to these external visibility drivers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content design focus versus targeting influentials
rubrics_metrics.description: Crafting contagious content (via emotion, practical value, surprise, interest) may be more effective than targeting a few 'special' influentials for generating word-of-mouth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper argues (with citation to recent work challenging the influentials hypothesis) that focusing resources on content characteristics that increase transmission is likely to be more cost-effective than trying to locate and target special individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sharing context as a moderator (narrowcasting vs broadcasting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Audience size and mode of sharing moderate what content is shared: narrowcasting favors recipient-focused/ niche content; broadcasting favors self-focused/content that signals identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors suggest (direction for future work) that narrowcasting (e-mailing a friend) and broadcasting (posting publicly) likely have different motives and therefore different optimal content characteristics; this moderates how content features translate into sharing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tradeoffs: virality vs brand/product effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Activating negative emotions can increase transmission but may have adverse effects on brand or product attitudes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Marketers should weigh the benefit of increased sharing from anxiety/anger-inducing content against potential brand damage (citations on negative emotion hurting brand attitudes). Example: BMW's 'The Hire' used anxiety-inducing storylines and achieved high views, but brand effects should be considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational recommendation: identify emotion types in user-generated content
rubrics_metrics.description: Use textual analysis to distinguish different negative emotions (e.g., anger/anxiety vs sadness) to prioritize managerial responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because anxiety/anger are more likely to be shared than sadness, firms should monitor and respond preferentially to posts that evoke activating negative emotions. The paper notes sentiment/text analysis can help separate types of negative posts for triage.
